evidence_set: Chart review of all emergency visits to one Colorado university hospital, 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016: 449,031 eligible visits, 9,973 with a cannabis-related diagnosis code (the participants were adults with such a code), 2,567 (25.7% of the 9,973) judged at least partly attributable to cannabis. Route was recorded in 2,432 of the 2,567 (94.7%): 238 edible (9.3% of the 2,567; 9.8% of the 2,432) and 2,194 inhaled; the 135 visits with insufficient documentation were counted as inhaled, giving 2,329. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%). Cannabis use is assessed in the nursing assessment questionnaire and the providers' notes; the route was captured from the medical record, and inhalation was presumed when it was not documented. Visits attributable to inhaled and to edible cannabis both rose each year (Figure 2, an image, not read).

Table 2 counts, edible and inhaled: intoxication 115 and 647 (762 in all); acute psychiatric symptoms 43 and 254 (297); cardiovascular symptoms 19 and 73 (92); gastrointestinal symptoms 36 and 752; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 20 and 420. Editors' arithmetic: edible-attributed visits were 15.1%, 14.5% and 20.7% of the intoxication, acute psychiatric and cardiovascular visits, so most visits for those reasons were inhaled-attributed. Across the 2,567 visits (reasons not mutually exclusive): gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 788 (30.7%), of which cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 440 visits (17.1%) by 301 people; intoxication 762 (29.7%), psychiatric symptoms 633 (24.7%), cardiovascular symptoms 92 (3.6%).

Timing as described by the authors, citing a pharmacology review (Grotenhermen 2003, not read): inhaled cannabis gives clinical effects within 10 minutes, a peak blood concentration within 30 to 90 minutes and complete clearance within 4 hours; oral THC does not reach a significant blood concentration until at least 30 minutes, peaks at about 3 hours and clears about 12 hours after ingestion. People report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping (reference 8, Giombi 2018, on consumers' perceptions of edibles; its design is not stated on the page) and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms (reference 9, an analysis of Twitter posts); neither was read. Death has been associated with edible products in three cases taken from news reports (references 10 to 12). No timing was measured in this study's patients.

A narrative overview published by RTI Press (PMC lists it as Methods Rep RTI Press), written for the educated layperson and policy makers. The Abstract says little research has evaluated how ingestion differs from other methods of cannabis use in therapeutic efficacy, subjective effects and safety; that the most prominent difference between ingestion and inhalation of cannabis extracts is the delayed onset of drug effect with ingestion; and that consumers who do not understand this may consume more than intended before the effect starts, often resulting in profoundly adverse effects (no count is given). The Introduction says the authors describe promises and challenges and critically examine extant research; no search method, selection criteria or appraisal of studies is described.

After eating, liver first-pass metabolism forms 11-OH-THC, a potent psychoactive metabolite that appears in blood in higher quantities after ingestion than after inhalation (as cited); the authors write that it may be responsible for the stronger and longer-lasting effect of edibles compared with comparable doses of smoked cannabis. Inhaled THC takes initial effect within minutes and shows peak effect in about 20 to 30 minutes, with psychoactive effects tapering off within 2 to 3 hours; the initial psychoactive effect of edibles takes 30 to 90 minutes to be felt and the high is longer-lasting, with a peak 2 to 4 hours after ingestion (Grotenhermen 2003 and others, as cited, not read). Weight, metabolism, gender and eating habits are said to affect how soon and how long.

After oral doses, plasma THC is lower than after smoking or infusion, and its correlation with degree of intoxication varies considerably across individuals (Hollister 1981, as cited); oral bioavailability is 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (Schwilke 2009, as cited). The authors say the lack of consistency and the delayed intoxication may lead both new and experienced people to take more than intended, and write that edible products are responsible for the majority of health care visits due to cannabis intoxication, which they say is likely due to users' failure to appreciate the delayed effects (a 2015 JAMA article by Monte, Zane and Heard, as cited, not read).

Dosage estimation for retail products may be inexact (Vandrey 2015, as cited). Anecdotal reports from medicinal cannabis patients are said to confirm that even people who take cannabis daily may consume more than expected (Hudak 2015, a letter in the American Journal of Psychiatry, as cited): having eaten the suggested serving first, patients ate the entire product after not feeling any effects, and found it practical to eat the entire product in one sitting.

A 2014 newspaper investigation found the actual THC content of retail edibles often differed significantly from labels; from mid-2014 Colorado required THC in recreational edibles to be tested and labelled but tested only against a threshold, which does not check label accuracy. One study of medicinal edibles sold in California and Washington is reported to have found that the total THC content of 83 percent of edibles tested differed from the labelled amounts by over 10 percent, with more than half containing significantly less than claimed and nearly a quarter significantly more (Vandrey 2015, as cited; not read).

Children: in a review of US poison-centre data on unintentional exposures in young children (up to 9 years of age), cannabis-related calls rose 30.3 percent a year in decriminalized states, 11.5 percent in states undergoing transition to decriminalization and 1.5 percent in nonlegal states, 2005 to 2011 (Wang 2014, as cited), with similar increases in edible-related calls in 2013 to 2015 (Cao 2016, as cited). The authors write that emergency visits for child exposure remain relatively low: a Colorado children's hospital saw no cases of accidental ingestion in 2005 to 2009, eight children who ingested edible cannabis in 2013 and 14 in 2014 (a hospital-association web item, as cited). Visitors: out-of-town patient visits to an Aurora, Colorado hospital for problems after edibles almost doubled from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant difference for Colorado residents (Kim 2016, as cited; not read); that study's authors attributed the rise to higher potency and visitors' unfamiliarity with edibles. The reference list gives the letter's authors as Kim, Hall, Genco, Van Dyke, Barker and Monte (the first author of Monte 2019 is Monte).

On smoke: cannabis and tobacco smoke are said to be similar in kind in toxicity; cannabis smoke is linked to lung inflammation and bronchitis; the link to chronic lung disease is unclear; epidemiological research links habitual cannabis smoking to several cancers but is complicated by small samples and co-occurring tobacco smoking. The authors then write that eating edibles does not seem to affect lung function or raise cancer risk, calling this a solid rationale for choosing this route as opposed to smoking cannabis, particularly for medical conditions such as cancer. No study of people who eat cannabis is cited for the last point.
